newsitem.title: UK: BA strike threat red-alert, brand impact seen.
newsitem.headline: BA strike threat red-alert, brand impact seen.

text.p: British Airways was on red alert this week to combat the looming threat of strike action, unveiling plans for strong-arm tactics to keep services flying -- a move observers say could tarnish its new 60 million pounds ($99.8 million) rebranding as the world's "friendly" airline.

Tour operators said on Thursday they had detected no panic among travellers after BA cabin crew voted in favour of striking on Wednesday. But industry groups warned if a strike involving close to 5,000 cabin crew goes ahead, BA's services and image were bound to suffer.

"If the strike happens, people will be trying to get through picket lines. There will be hold-ups, delays and confusion and BA may lose business in the long term over this," said a spokeswoman for the Association of Independent Tour Operators.
Keith Betton, director of the Association of British Travel Agents, told Reuters he was unaware of anyone switching flights yet.
"But people are phoning to ask what to do if there is a strike. If it goes ahead it will cost BA a lot of money."
BA's newly-launched image makeover, announced to much fanfare earlier this month, is also likely to be damaged if a strike date is set next week, analysts said.
"The potential for harm is very high," said Andy Milligan, director of global branding consultancy Interbrand which advises Swiss Air and Germany's Lufthansa.

"BA has just announced to the world that it is changing. It's friendly, customer focused and this message has come at a time when it is under intense scrutiny over how it treats its staff -- the people on which that brand image is built."
"If its staff feel used and abused, BA will have a major problem delivering its brand message," Milligan said.
Unions representing three quarters of BA's 12,000 cabin crew announced on Wednesday that 73 percent of the ballot was in favour of strike action over a bitter five-month long pay row.

The final decision on whether to strike and for how long will be taken on Monday. But BA faces a separate strike ballot result covering 9,000 ground staff on Tuesday over the disputed sale of the catering unit, which employs 1,200 staff.
BA has responded by warning that all strikers face loss of perks, promotion and may even be sued for loss of business if a strike goes ahead.

A battle plan for dealing with the strike has been drawn up for some time, offering strike breakers 75 pounds in cash per day for travelling to work, hotel accommodation and meeting points for coaches to drive workers through picket lines.
On top of that comes the heavy cost of external security to monitor picket lines.
One travel industry insider said they sounded more like plans for a "mini-war" than an airline.
BA has refused to quantify the potential cost of such measures. "The cost is not the important factor," said a BA spokesman. "It is to keep the airline flying."
BA chief executive, Robert Ayling said late Wednesday the company "will not be held back by 1970s-style trade unionism" in efforts to restructure.
It hopes to rely on 3,000 cabin crew which have already backed the pay deal and said there were 1,500 non-unionised staff.
"We are training managers and staff to take on other roles and there is the possibility of taking on help from outside the airline," said the BA spokesman.
But the T&G said BA's adoption of a "scab army" to fill strikers' jobs would harm services.
Even before a strike has been officially called, British papers were drawing possible comparisons with the vicious stand-offs seen in the 1980s miners' strike.
"The difference with the miners' strike, however, was that no single brand was suffering from the bad publicity," Interbrand's Milligan said.

Flights possibly affected by a strike include mainline services from Heathrow and some continental flights from Gatwick -- hitting Britain's two biggest airports. But BA said flights on the CityFlyer Express franchise would be unaffected.
If unions vote for a strike, BA must receive seven days' notice and the action must be held within 24 days of the ballot. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
